children: Anthropic is at last pulling the trigger on its once-delayed IPO — a relief to venture investors and their limited-partner backers, who also hope the massive sale could have a ripple effect in ending a long dry spell in cash returns.
Unlike SpaceX, which went public in June some 24 years after its founding, Anthropic, at just five years of age, has lurched from launch to public listing — and at monumental scale.

Hundreds of venture funds, including Spark Capital, Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners, hold Anthropic stock, according to PitchBook, so the impact of its initial public offering will be meaningful for many market participants.

"In this case, significant gains will go to younger funds, which should help the liquidity crunch for many LPs who were newer entrants or newer to scale VC exposure this decade," said Aakar Vachhani, managing partner at investment firm Fairview Capital, referring to venture funds of recent vintage years. Several venture funds that Fairview backs are investors in Anthropic.

While AI startups have been raising capital at a rapid pace, cash has been slow to return to the pockets of investors. The SpaceX IPO, as well as recent startup acquisitions, began to change that dynamic. Now many hope Anthropic will bring more of it.

"Anthropic is expected to produce even more liquidity that LPs can use to fund new VC fund commitments," said John Zeratsky, co-founder and general partner of Character Capital, who doesn't own Anthropic stock.

As some raise doubts over the frothy state of AI markets and compare them to previous bubbles, Anthropic's financials gave some credibility to those who believe generative AI startups can gap far larger, and faster, than businesses of the past.

"Seeing that kind of growth is what venture dreams are made of," said Roseanne Wincek, co-founder and managing director of venture firm Renegade Partners. Renegade isn't an investor in Anthropic, but Wincek has some exposure via a special-purpose vehicle.
In the S-1 public-offering documents released Monday, Anthropic said it generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first six months of this year, up from $1.2 billion in the year-prior period.
"There were a few pleasant surprises in the S-1, but mostly it's in line with what everyone hoped and expected," Zeratsky said.

The filing of the S-1 suggests the company is confident it can pull off what's expected to be a mammoth IPO before Thanksgiving, said Louis Lehot, a partner at the law firm of Foley & Lardner. That's despite a jittery market, rising interest rates, coming elections and a popular backlash against data centers.
"This means they absolutely intend on going out," Lehot said.

Though Anthropic's S-1 warns of the potential harms of the technology — even contemplating an uninsurable "catastrophic AI-related event" — VCs focused on the IPO as a financial fulcrum. And the Anthropic IPO will likely make the AI faithful even more open to underwriting high-valuation deals.
"There's going to be even more exuberance," commented Wincek.
Anthropic, of course, still has to deliver on its IPO. And for the next month or so, everyone will be watching and waiting.
"I don't think there is a market other than Anthropic right now," Lehot said of tech IPOs. "No one can get anything done in tech until this is done."
